references.title: Formatting Your Spec Script While Social Distancing: A Primer, Part 1
references.note: Observed pages, scenes, acts and conventions of ten TV scripts; descriptive house style, some from one pilot.

references.title: TV Format Fundamentals: Serialized Drama
references.note: Four acts or four plus a teaser; acts exist whether or not they are marked; match the show's page convention.

references.title: Medium and Format
references.note: One broadcaster's submission norms: sitcom episodes are 30 minutes, say whether a script is for live studio recording.

references.title: Sample script formats: three-camera sitcom and taped sitcom
references.note: Teaser, lettered scenes, capitals action, double-spaced dialogue; the taped-sitcom sample (bbctapedsitcom.pdf) leaves wide margins for studio cues. PDF text lost its indents.

references.title: Sample script formats: stage, UK and US
references.note: UK and US stage layouts (the US one is stageus.pdf); stage action limited to set and events, never character thoughts or backstory.

references.title: Scriptwriting Essentials: 6. Scenes
references.note: A scene is a significant change, not an explanation; four questions to ask of every scene.

references.title: Scriptwriting Essentials: 7. Dialogue
references.note: Dialogue is not conversation; on-the-nose and expositional dialogue is the commonest fault; individuated voices; sparing dialect.

references.title: Scriptwriting Essentials: 3. Beginnings (and Endings)
references.note: Open with characters in action; make them want something and pursue it.

references.title: Short and sweet? Structuring Humor and Morality in American Sitcoms
references.note: Close reading of sitcom structure; quotes a 2014 magazine joke-per-minute count for twelve shows; the laugh-track pace reading is the author's interpretation.

references.title: Contagious laughter: Laughter is a sufficient stimulus for laughs and smiles
references.note: Four-page classroom experiment, 128 students: recorded laughter prompted laughing at first and wore out by the tenth playback; no jokes involved.

references.title: Long scripts don't necessarily mean long movies
references.note: The page-per-minute rule barely works in aggregate and is not predictive for one project; script timing is better.

references.title: Desperate punchlines
references.note: Second-hand: one showrunner's instruction not to end a line on its funniest word.

references.title: The Book of Acts
references.note: Hour dramas moving from four to five acts; count the turns; early acts run longer than late ones.

references.title: Cognitive scientists 1, screenplay gurus 0
references.note: Four-part model of classical Hollywood features against three acts; a shot-length study is reported second-hand.

references.title: Free downloadable script formats for plays and musicals
references.note: Formats are guidelines, not requirements; 12-point Courier; character page; no right way to end a scene; no pages-per-minute figure.

references.title: Modern and traditional play format templates and the general formatting guide
references.note: Name and direction layouts differ between the two templates (modernformat-New.pdf, traditionalformat-New.pdf) and the general guide, which is of unstated origin.

references.authors: Greg Beal (Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences)
references.title: Screenplay format guide for the Nicholl Fellowships
references.note: Feature layout; short description paragraphs; manner-of-speech parentheticals frowned upon; no absolute standard format.

references.title: Joke Writing Workshop
references.note: Topical jokes with topic handles and associations; the capture is an index page with every breakdown cut off.

references.authors: A. Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren
references.title: Benign violations: Making immoral behavior funny
references.note: Five small studies (N 36 to 80) of moral-violation scenarios: amusement needs a violation seen as benign.

references.title: Is the concept of incongruity still a useful construct for the advancement of humor research?
references.note: Theoretical review: incongruity is necessary but not sufficient; full resolution ends the humour.

references.title: How funny is ChatGPT? A comparison of human- and A.I.-produced jokes
references.note: Two pre-registered studies of ChatGPT 3.5 with example-rich prompts and blind lay ratings; model had 20 tries per prompt.

references.title: ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny! Humor is still challenging Large Language Models
references.note: Over 90% of 1008 generated jokes were the same 25; abstract only.
